analysis.one_liner: Requires emergency refuges, communications, tracking devices, and steeper fines to protect underground coal miners.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on May 12, 2006, the mine safety bill was referred to committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal mine safety law to help underground coal miners survive emergencies. It required oxygen caches, underground refuges stocked for five days, two-way communications, atmospheric monitoring, and electronic tracking of miners, and it lifted the limit on how many federal mine inspectors could be hired. It also raised fines for safety violations, made ignoring a pattern of violations punishable by up to $1 million, created a confidential ombudsman for miners to report dangers, and cut the legal limit on coal dust that causes black lung disease.
analysis.who_benefits: Underground coal miners and their families gain the most: the bill's escape and rescue requirements directly address how miners died in the 2006 mine disasters, when rescuers could not locate trapped men and communications failed. Miners also gain a confidential channel to report unsafe conditions, a lower dust limit that reduces black lung disease, and an independent investigation option when a disaster kills their coworkers. Mine rescue teams and regulators gain clearer requirements and more inspectors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Underground coal miners and their families

how_it_helps.text: Mine operators would have to install underground refuges that every miner can reach within 15 minutes, each stocked with enough air, food, and water for five days and with two-way communication to the surface.

Within 30 days of enactment, operators would have to place emergency caches of air and breathing equipment throughout mines, spaced no farther apart than a 30-minute walk, plus self-rescue devices, training on them, and flame-retardant lifelines.

Operators would have to install atmospheric monitoring for methane, carbon monoxide, and oxygen; provide miners with emergency message devices and, once certified, two-way underground-surface radios; and give every miner an electronic tracking device so rescuers can find them.
Ceilings on the number of MSHA mine inspectors would be abolished for five years, and retired inspectors could be hired to prevent a staffing gap during a wave of retirements.

Fines would rise sharply: up to $250,000 per violation (up to $500,000 for serious safety-standard violations), up to $1,000,000 for a pattern of violations with corporate owners jointly liable, and a felony with a $50,000 fine or one year in prison for failing to pay assessed penalties; operators would have to report emergencies within 15 minutes or face penalties of at least $60,000.

A Miner Ombudsman within the Labor Department's Inspector General office would take confidential reports of safety problems from miners, and violations of the new emergency standards would count as creating imminent danger, letting inspectors pull miners out immediately.

The legal limit on respirable coal dust would drop to 1.0 milligram per cubic meter, measured by regulators rather than operators, to reduce black lung disease, and the bill would tighten standards for conveyor-belt flammability and for seals blocking abandoned mine areas.
Families of miners killed in an accident could request an independent federal investigation, and a family advocate would keep them included in official investigations.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators pay: they must buy and install communications, tracking, and atmospheric-monitoring equipment, oxygen caches, refuges, and flame-retardant lifelines, pay a $100 user fee on each penalty assessed, and absorb much higher fines, joint liability for corporate owners, and possible felony exposure for unpaid penalties. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed on in coal and electricity prices. The Mine Safety and Health Administration also needs money to staff a 24-hour emergency call center, inspect seals, and hire more inspectors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators, through equipment and fines

drawbacks.text: The compliance deadlines are extremely tight: oxygen caches and maintenance programs were due within 30 days of enactment, refuges within a year, and tracking and warning systems within 180 days, which would strain smaller mines' budgets and logistics even though the safety case for the equipment is strong.

The bill writes detailed technical standards directly into statute with fixed deadlines, bypassing the usual rulemaking process where engineers, operators, and safety experts normally work out what is feasible; the standards could be superseded only through a formal modification procedure.

The enforcement provisions are unusually harsh for occupational-safety law: failing to timely pay any penalty becomes a felony punishable by a $50,000 fine or one year in prison, a $1 million pattern-of-violations penalty is jointly and severally liable on all owners and cannot be reduced by the review commission, and escrow of contested penalties is required within 30 days.

Operators who are fined must pay a $100 user fee per penalty, and the bill bars the Labor Department from giving operators technical support or advice except through that fee-funded program, which small operators could find burdensome.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strong: the escape, refuge, communications, and tracking requirements aim squarely at the failures that killed miners in 2006, and the dust and seal provisions address known health and explosion hazards. The costs fall on an industry whose product already carries large external risks, and equipment requirements of this kind were later adopted for underground coal mines. The bill's weaknesses are design, not substance: rigid statutory deadlines and unusually severe criminal penalties for late payment would have been better calibrated through ordinary rulemaking, and small mines would feel the compliance burden most.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on May 12, 2006, joined by Senators Rockefeller, Murray, and Durbin, months after a string of deadly mine accidents.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Kennedy delivered introductory remarks on May 15, 2006, and that was the last action of any kind on the bill.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory purchases of refuges, communications, tracking, and monitoring equipment, the fivefold increase in maximum fines, joint corporate-owner liability, and the felony penalty for unpaid fines. Miners got none of the new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators, who avoided the new safety costs

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Patty Murray and Dick Durbin

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership under Chair Mike Enzi
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred bill sat in the committee for the rest of the Congress; the chair never scheduled a hearing or markup and the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no vote was ever taken, so whether support would have split by party was never tested.

industries.note: Operators would have borne the full cost of refuges, oxygen caches, communications and tracking equipment, and fivefold-higher fines with joint liability for corporate owners and felony exposure for unpaid penalties. The bill's premise is that operators' cost of these protections is worth bearing to keep miners alive.

industries.industry: Mining communications, tracking, and safety equipment makers
industries.note: The bill creates immediate demand for two-way underground communications devices, electronic tracking tags, atmospheric monitors, refuges, and improved self-rescuers, and directs faster federal approval of new safety technologies.

industries.industry: Mine Safety and Health Administration (federal mine inspectors)
industries.note: The bill lifts the personnel ceiling on inspectors for five years, lets the agency rehire retired inspectors, and adds a 24-hour emergency call center, expanding the enforcement workforce that watches over operators.
